findings.issue_text: organization_context is referenced at src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py:71 (organization_context.member.has_global_access) but never defined anywhere in the endpoint's get() method or created by the diff, so every request to /organizations/<slug>/audit-logs/ raises NameError and a 500, breaking the audit log endpoint for all organizations.

The enable_advanced expression at organization_auditlogs.py:71 is evaluated unconditionally before the if use_optimized and enable_advanced: check instead of being placed inside the use_optimized branch, so it runs on every audit-log GET even for requests that never pass optimized_pagination=true, and any case where .member is None (e.g., a superuser without an OrganizationMember row) raises AttributeError on every request.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key (src/sentry/api/paginator.py:838-840) applies math.floor/math.ceil to a datetime value (the paginator is instantiated with order_by='-datetime'), which always raises TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime; the class omits the timegm(value.utctimetuple()) timestamp conversion that DateTimePaginator uses, so any authorized user passing optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 on the first paginated request whenever the organization has any audit entries.

Negative-offset slicing crashes because Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts that slice starts are non-negative, so queryset[start_offset:stop] with cursor.offset < 0 raises AssertionError; the comment at src/sentry/api/paginator.py:877-882 (and the base-class comment at lines 179-181) claiming the ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically is factually wrong, and since build_cursor never emits negative offsets the branch is reachable only via hand-forged cursors (unsigned base64 JSON), so the PR's headline capability is unreachable in legitimate flows and its only reachable behavior is an unhandled AssertionError 500 for the privileged users it is gated to.

Even hypothetically, on a list-backed queryset negative slicing means slicing from the end of the dataset (a different result set than requested), and the follow-up trim check len(results) == offset + limit + extra at src/sentry/api/paginator.py:~891 is arithmetically wrong for negative offset, so prev-cursors would be computed from the wrong boundary.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor (src/sentry/api/paginator.py:842-843) returns the raw cursor value instead of converting the integer back to a datetime as DateTimePaginator does (datetime.fromtimestamp(cursor.value, timezone.utc)), so build_queryset receives datetime__lt=<int> against a DateTimeField and Django raises ValidationError during query construction, meaning every cursor-following request (page 2 and beyond) on the optimized path would 500 or filter against a meaningless integer comparison.

The base paginator change at src/sentry/api/paginator.py:182-184 modifies the shared BasePaginator.get_result used by every paginator in the application, not just this feature, and handles invalid cursors with negative offsets inconsistently between directions: next-direction cursors are now silently clamped to offset 0 (previously raising a loud AssertionError), so the client receives page 1 of the dataset as if nothing were wrong, while prev-direction cursors are not clamped and still raise AssertionError, globally converting an invalid-input error into silently-incorrect success.

`organization_context` is never defined in `organization_auditlogs.py` (the endpoint method receives `organization`), so the expression `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises `NameError` → HTTP 500; the line runs unconditionally rather than being gated on `optimized_pagination=true`, so every non-superuser request to the audit-logs endpoint fails

Even if `organization_context` resolved, the access check is still wrong: `OrganizationMember` has no `has_global_access` attribute, and the permission check should go through `request.access`/permission classes rather than a bare member lookup

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` extends `BasePaginator` but never implements `get_query_params` (which raises `NotImplementedError`), even though `get_result` calls `build_queryset`; any request carrying a cursor with a value (page 2, next, prev) therefore raises `NotImplementedError` → 500, and the paginator cannot filter by cursor at all — the copy of `DateTimePaginator.get_result` omitted the `get_query_params` override that supplies `datetime__lt/__gt` cursor filtering

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` drops `DateTimePaginator`'s datetime↔timestamp conversion: with `order_by='-datetime'`, `getattr(item, 'datetime')` is a `datetime` object and `math.floor(<datetime>)` raises `TypeError` in `build_cursor`, so even page 1 of the optimized path crashes

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value (an int timestamp) instead of converting it to a `datetime` as `DateTimePaginator` does, so even with a `get_query_params` present the queryset filter would compare a datetime column against an int

Negative-offset slicing is impossible in the Django ORM (`QuerySet[negative:…]` raises 'Negative indexing is not supported'), so the `cursor.offset < 0` branch in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` can only raise an exception, contradicting the comment's claim that Django handles negative slicing automatically; the branch is reachable because cursors are unsigned client-supplied base64 JSON and `Cursor.__init__` accepts any negative `int(offset)`, so an opted-in admin sending a crafted cursor gets a 500

The clamp added to the shared `get_result` (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`) is dead code for legitimate traffic since `build_cursor` only ever produces non-negative offsets, and it only clamps non-prev cursors, leaving the pre-existing negative-offset crash in place for crafted prev cursors — the change neither fixes the claimed problem nor enables anything

The PR delivers no actual performance improvement: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` executes the identical `list(queryset[start:stop])` offset-slice and the same `build_cursor` flow as the existing `DateTimePaginator` — same query shape, materialization, and scan characteristics — with no unbounded-query fix, reduced materialization, or algorithmic change; the cursor filtering that actually keeps cursor pagination cheap is precisely what the new class is missing
The identity-gated optimized path produces divergent pagination behavior for different users hitting the same URL
`enable_advanced_features` is a dead constructor flag — it is hardcoded to `True` at the only call site, so it serves no gating purpose

The stated goal of audit-log pagination performance should be pursued via index/covering-query work on the `AuditLogEntry` ordering key or a true keyset (non-offset) cursor path, rather than a duplicated paginator class

[P0] organization_context is undefined in src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py:71 — enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access executes unconditionally on every GET (it is not inside the if use_optimized guard, so short-circuiting doesn't help, and the symbol is neither defined in get() nor imported anywhere in this diff), so every request to the audit-logs endpoint raises a NameError and returns a 500, causing total availability loss of the public org audit-log API for Sentry's UI and external API consumers.

[P1] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil to a datetime — the endpoint passes order_by='-datetime', so getattr(item, 'datetime') on an AuditLogEntry returns a datetime.datetime, and math.floor(value)/math.ceil(value) on a datetime raises TypeError; get_item_key is invoked by build_cursor (and the prev-edge trim) whenever at least one row is returned, so the optimized path can never complete once reachable (a privileged caller sending optimized_pagination=true against a non-empty log gets a 500), and the floored/ceiled int cursor values are semantically incompatible with DateTimePaginator's timestamp cursors.

[P1] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key also relies on self._is_asc existing on BasePaginator; if the attribute doesn't exist, an AttributeError is raised even earlier — the same non-functional outcome for the optimized path.

[P1] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result calls self.build_queryset(...), which the class — extending BasePaginator directly and defining no build_queryset — never implements; it is abstract (NotImplementedError) on BasePaginator, and unlike OffsetPaginator/DateTimePaginator whose get_result never calls it, this get_result calls it before slicing, so every request through this paginator raises before any data is fetched; additionally, build_queryset(0, False) on a first-page cursor (value 0) would filter datetime > 0, semantics that need explicit review rather than silent inheritance.

[P2] The negative-offset 'advanced feature' always raises — queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset < 0 raises from Django's QuerySet ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so any negative-offset cursor on this path produces a 500 rather than 'efficient bidirectional pagination', and the comments at paginator.py ~179-181 and ~874-886 falsely claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' will mislead future maintainers and reviewers.

[P2] Shared OffsetPaginator.get_result silently changes behavior for negative-offset cursors API-wide with no per-caller audit: non-prev cursors are silently clamped to 0 and served page-1 data while build_cursor derives the next cursor from the unclamped negative offset (offset -5 with limit 100 serves rows 0-99 but emits a next cursor at offset 95, duplicating rows), and prev cursors with negative offsets still pass the negative value into slicing and crash — the same invalid input class (cursors are client-supplied unsigned base64 JSON, so negative offsets are client-reachable) now yields two different outcomes across the many public endpoints backed by OffsetPaginator/DateTimePaginator, producing silently wrong data and corrupt Link-header cursors instead of a clean failure.

[P2] One public route now serves two incompatible cursor contracts selected by an undocumented query param and the caller's identity: DateTimePaginator pages purely by offset (cursor.value used only for prev-edge trimming) while OptimizedCursorPaginator filters by cursor.value and also applies the offset, so a Link-header cursor emitted under one path and replayed under the other (client drops optimized_pagination=true when following the link, link shared with a non-superuser, or the is_superuser/global-access gate differs between callers) is reinterpreted under different semantics, producing skipped or duplicated rows — same route, same token, different results per caller, with no versioning and no documentation of the new param, breaking any client that caches or shares pagination links.

[P3] The cursors.py change is comment-only and misstates the input contract — comments at src/sentry/utils/cursors.py:26-27 claim negative offsets are now 'allowed ... for advanced pagination', but self.offset = int(offset) is byte-identical to before with no validation added and no behavior changed, documenting an externally reachable input contract that nothing implements while omitting the one coherent change (rejecting negative offsets in decode_cursor) that the negative-offset issues would actually have needed.

[P3] Paginator-specific constructor kwarg enable_advanced_features=True is pushed through the shared Endpoint.paginate() boundary at organization_auditlogs.py:82 — if paginate() does not forward arbitrary kwargs to the paginator constructor, this either raises TypeError (another 500 on the optimized path) or silently drops the flag, making the negative-offset branch at paginator.py ~877 permanently unreachable; needs verification against Endpoint.paginate's signature.

In src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py:71, `organization_context` is never defined (the endpoint receives `organization`), so `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises NameError for every non-superuser (org owners, API-key clients) on every GET of the audit-logs endpoint — the line executes unconditionally (not gated by `use_optimized`) and only superusers avoid evaluating the second operand via `or` short-circuiting, causing a guaranteed 500 on this compliance-critical endpoint regardless of the optimized_pagination flag.

Even setting the NameError aside, `.member.has_global_access` in that line matches no real permission attribute, and the endpoint's `OrganizationAuditPermission` already gates access, so the permission check is broken and redundant even in its intended form.

Django `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `AssertionError` ('Negative indexing is not supported') on negative slice bounds, so the paginator's negative-offset slicing (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` in the advanced branch at paginator.py ~888-891 and the unclamped `is_prev` paths at ~898 and ~182) always results in an unhandled 500 — the comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false, and since legitimate cursors never carry negative offsets (only forged, unsigned base64 cursors, which `Cursor.__init__` happily accepts negative ints for), the advertised negative-offset pagination feature is only reachable as a crash and can never return a successful response.

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` calls `self.build_queryset(cursor_value, cursor.is_prev)` (~858) as the first paginator call in `get_result`, but `build_queryset` was never copied or defined — it is a `DateTimePaginator` method not provided by `BasePaginator` — so every optimized request raises AttributeError immediately.

The `get_item_key` copied into `OptimizedCursorPaginator` dropped the datetime-to-number normalization its `DateTimePaginator` source has: with `order_by='-datetime'`, `math.floor(<datetime>)` / `math.ceil(<datetime>)` raises TypeError the first time it is invoked (prev-dedup at ~891 or inside `build_cursor`) on any non-empty page, and using key='id' instead would dedup/build cursors on `pk` while ordering by `datetime` — wrong keyset pagination, so no configuration of the copied code is correct.

`enable_advanced_features=True` is passed to `Endpoint.paginate()` (organization_auditlogs.py:77-85), which has a fixed parameter list (`request, queryset, paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, count_hits, known_hits, max_hits`) and does not forward unknown kwargs to `paginator_cls`, raising TypeError before the paginator is even instantiated — an independent, earlier crash on the optimized path.

Double pagination in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` (paginator.py ~885-898): `build_queryset` applies a keyset filter truncating the queryset to rows past the cursor value, then the already-filtered queryset is offset-sliced (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`) while `build_cursor` advances the cursor's offset by `limit` every page — on page 2 the code slices `[limit : 2*limit]` of the rows older than the boundary, silently skipping the entire next page of audit entries.

The prev-boundary dedup check `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` (paginator.py ~894) compares against a window that no longer matches the actual slice whenever clamping/negative offsets are in play, producing duplicate boundary rows.

The `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` change in shared `OffsetPaginator.get_result` (paginator.py ~181-185) silently masks invalid cursors: it is a no-op for all legitimate cursors (so the optimization does nothing for real traffic), but forged negative-offset cursors that previously triggered a loud `AssertionError`/500 are now silently clamped to 0 and return 200 OK with page-1 data while `build_cursor` keeps advancing the cursor chain from the unclamped negative offset, yielding repeated/duplicated pages and a corrupted cursor sequence; because this edits the shared `OffsetPaginator`, the blast radius is every offset-paginated endpoint in the API (members, projects, etc.), not just audit logs, and no boundary validation was added anywhere.

The clamping is inconsistent between the two branches of the same change: the forward path clamps negative offsets to 0 while the `is_prev` branch deliberately leaves them unclamped, so the identical forged input silently returns a 200 in one branch and still crashes with `AssertionError` in the other.

On the same endpoint and URL, paginator selection (`DateTimePaginator` vs `OptimizedCursorPaginator`) depends on a client-controlled query param and the user's class, producing different cursor value encodings (raw passthrough vs normalized datetime keys) and offset semantics; a cursor minted by one path and replayed against the other (param toggled mid-pagination, or a shared/bookmarked URL) is silently misinterpreted — wrong pages, no error — and responses are non-reproducible across users for the same query.

adjudication.rationale: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is used by `organization_auditlogs` with `order_by="-datetime"` (a datetime column), but its cursor handling is numeric: `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged and `get_item_key` applies `math.floor/ceil` to `getattr(item, self.key)`. Unlike `DateTimePaginator` (implied by the finding) there is no conversion from an int cursor value into a `datetime` for queryset filtering, so filtering a datetime field with an int cursor value would be incorrect/broken when this paginator is enabled.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Negative-offset slicing is impossible in the Django ORM (`QuerySet[negative:…]` raises 'Negative indexing is not supported'), so the `cursor.offset < 0` branch in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` can only raise an exception, contradicting the comment's claim that Django handles negative slicing automatically; the branch is reachable because cursors are unsigned client-supplied base64 JSON and `Cursor.__init__` accepts any negative `int(offset)`, so an opted-in admin sending a crafted cursor gets a 500

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the `if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0:` branch slices the queryset with `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset` is negative (`start_offset = cursor.offset`). Django `QuerySet` slicing does not support negative indexes and will raise an exception, so this path can produce a 500. The diff also makes negative offsets possible from client-supplied cursors by accepting any `int(offset)` in `Cursor.__init__` (commented as allowing negative offsets), and the endpoint can enable this paginator for opted-in admins via `optimized_pagination=true` plus `enable_advanced_features=True`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The clamp added to the shared `get_result` (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`) is dead code for legitimate traffic since `build_cursor` only ever produces non-negative offsets, and it only clamps non-prev cursors, leaving the pre-existing negative-offset crash in place for crafted prev cursors — the change neither fixes the claimed problem nor enables anything

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py#get_result`, the new clamp only applies when `not cursor.is_prev` (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`), so a request/crafted cursor with `is_prev=true` and a negative `cursor.offset` will still lead to `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices and will raise, so the “negative offset” path can still crash for prev cursors. The finding’s claim that this is dead code for legitimate traffic depends on `build_cursor` behavior, which is not shown in the diff, but the unhandled crafted-prev negative-offset crash is directly implied by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The PR delivers no actual performance improvement: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` executes the identical `list(queryset[start:stop])` offset-slice and the same `build_cursor` flow as the existing `DateTimePaginator` — same query shape, materialization, and scan characteristics — with no unbounded-query fix, reduced materialization, or algorithmic change; the cursor filtering that actually keeps cursor pagination cheap is precisely what the new class is missing

adjudication.rationale: The finding makes specific claims that aren’t supported by the diff. `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` does not “miss” cursor filtering; it explicitly computes `cursor_value` and calls `self.build_queryset(cursor_value, cursor.is_prev)`, which is the standard hook where cursor-based filtering is applied. The diff also does not show `DateTimePaginator`’s implementation, so it’s not verifiable from the PR that the new paginator is “identical” in query shape/scan characteristics to `DateTimePaginator`. While both implementations do a queryset slice and then call `build_cursor`, that alone doesn’t substantiate the claim that there is no algorithmic difference or that the key cursor-cheap filtering is absent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The identity-gated optimized path produces divergent pagination behavior for different users hitting the same URL

adjudication.rationale: The endpoint now conditionally switches paginator implementations based on user identity: `use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` and `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, using `OptimizedCursorPaginator` only when both are true, otherwise `DateTimePaginator`. This makes the same URL (including `optimized_pagination=true` and any cursor params) potentially yield different pagination semantics/links depending on who calls it, which is a concrete divergence introduced by the diff. Whether intentional (admin-only optimization) or not, it’s a real review concern because it can affect API consistency and cursor/link shareability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `enable_advanced_features` is a dead constructor flag — it is hardcoded to `True` at the only call site, so it serves no gating purpose

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, the only shown use of `OptimizedCursorPaginator` passes `enable_advanced_features=True` unconditionally (in `organization_auditlogs.py`), and `enable_advanced_features` is only used to gate the negative-offset branch inside `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`. As introduced here, the flag doesn’t meaningfully gate behavior at the call site (it’s always enabled whenever this paginator is selected), making it potentially redundant/over-designed in the scope of this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The stated goal of audit-log pagination performance should be pursued via index/covering-query work on the `AuditLogEntry` ordering key or a true keyset (non-offset) cursor path, rather than a duplicated paginator class

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` in `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` that largely duplicates existing paginator logic (custom `get_result` with slicing/offset handling) and wires it into `organization_auditlogs.py` behind `optimized_pagination=true` for admins. The finding’s core point—this performance goal would be better served by a true keyset path / indexing work rather than introducing a parallel paginator implementation—is a concrete architecture/scope concern created by this change (code duplication and alternate pagination behavior) rather than a directly verifiable correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [P0] organization_context is undefined in src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py:71 — enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access executes unconditionally on every GET (it is not inside the if use_optimized guard, so short-circuiting doesn't help, and the symbol is neither defined in get() nor imported anywhere in this diff), so every request to the audit-logs endpoint raises a NameError and returns a 500, causing total availability loss of the public org audit-log API for Sentry's UI and external API consumers.

adjudication.rationale: In `organization_auditlogs.py`, the new line `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` introduces a reference to `organization_context`, but the diff shows no local definition or import for `organization_context`. This expression is evaluated unconditionally before the `if use_optimized and enable_advanced:` guard, so if `organization_context` is not defined elsewhere in the module, it will raise `NameError` on every GET request to this endpoint.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [P1] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil to a datetime — the endpoint passes order_by='-datetime', so getattr(item, 'datetime') on an AuditLogEntry returns a datetime.datetime, and math.floor(value)/math.ceil(value) on a datetime raises TypeError; get_item_key is invoked by build_cursor (and the prev-edge trim) whenever at least one row is returned, so the optimized path can never complete once reachable (a privileged caller sending optimized_pagination=true against a non-empty log gets a 500), and the floored/ceiled int cursor values are semantically incompatible with DateTimePaginator's timestamp cursors.

adjudication.rationale: In the optimized path, `organization_auditlogs.py` calls `self.paginate(... paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, order_by="-datetime", ...)`, so the paginator will be keyed off the `datetime` field. `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key()` does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` and then applies `math.floor`/`math.ceil` and `int(...)`. If `self.key` is `"datetime"`, `value` will be a `datetime.datetime` (e.g., on `AuditLogEntry`), and `math.floor(value)`/`math.ceil(value)` will raise `TypeError`. This method is invoked in `get_result()` (the prev-edge trim and via `build_cursor`), so any non-empty result set on the optimized path would 500 once reachable via `optimized_pagination=true` for an eligible caller.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [P1] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key also relies on self._is_asc existing on BasePaginator; if the attribute doesn't exist, an AttributeError is raised even earlier — the same non-functional outcome for the optimized path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calling self._is_asc(for_prev), but it does not show BasePaginator (or any mixin) to determine whether _is_asc exists. The finding asserts an AttributeError will occur, which cannot be verified from the provided diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [P1] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result calls self.build_queryset(...), which the class — extending BasePaginator directly and defining no build_queryset — never implements; it is abstract (NotImplementedError) on BasePaginator, and unlike OffsetPaginator/DateTimePaginator whose get_result never calls it, this get_result calls it before slicing, so every request through this paginator raises before any data is fetched; additionally, build_queryset(0, False) on a first-page cursor (value 0) would filter datetime > 0, semantics that need explicit review rather than silent inheritance.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the newly added `OptimizedCursorPaginator` subclasses `BasePaginator` and its `get_result()` unconditionally calls `self.build_queryset(cursor_value, cursor.is_prev)`, but `OptimizedCursorPaginator` itself does not define `build_queryset`. Whether this works depends entirely on `BasePaginator` providing a concrete implementation; if `BasePaginator.build_queryset` is abstract/raises (as is common for base paginator classes), any request using `paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator` (added in `organization_auditlogs.py`) will fail before slicing. The finding’s core point (new class calls an unimplemented method relative to what’s shown) is directly grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [P2] The negative-offset 'advanced feature' always raises — queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset < 0 raises from Django's QuerySet ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so any negative-offset cursor on this path produces a 500 rather than 'efficient bidirectional pagination', and the comments at paginator.py ~179-181 and ~874-886 falsely claiming 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' will mislead future maintainers and reviewers.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces paths that slice a Django QuerySet with a negative start index. In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, it sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` and does `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which (in Django) raises “Negative indexing is not supported” for negative slice starts. Additionally, the earlier change in `paginator.py` also preserves negative `offset` when `cursor.is_prev` (`start_offset = ... else offset`), so negative offsets can still reach slicing. The comments claiming the ORM “properly handles negative slicing automatically” are therefore misleading, and this would produce a 500 on such cursors.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [P2] Shared OffsetPaginator.get_result silently changes behavior for negative-offset cursors API-wide with no per-caller audit: non-prev cursors are silently clamped to 0 and served page-1 data while build_cursor derives the next cursor from the unclamped negative offset (offset -5 with limit 100 serves rows 0-99 but emits a next cursor at offset 95, duplicating rows), and prev cursors with negative offsets still pass the negative value into slicing and crash — the same invalid input class (cursors are client-supplied unsigned base64 JSON, so negative offsets are client-reachable) now yields two different outcomes across the many public endpoints backed by OffsetPaginator/DateTimePaginator, producing silently wrong data and corrupt Link-header cursors instead of a clean failure.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` the shared `get_result` logic was changed to clamp `start_offset = max(0, offset)` only for non-`prev` cursors, but it still passes the original `cursor` (with the original possibly-negative `cursor.offset`) into `build_cursor(...)`. This can yield mismatched pagination: a negative `offset` will fetch from `0:...` while cursor generation may still advance from the negative offset, producing incorrect/duplicative next/prev cursors. Also, for `cursor.is_prev` the code keeps `start_offset = offset` (can be negative) and slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which in Django can raise on negative slicing. Since `Cursor.offset` is now explicitly allowed to be negative (`int(offset)` with a comment in `utils/cursors.py`), this invalid input is client-reachable and can cause silent wrong data or crashes across endpoints using this paginator.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [P2] One public route now serves two incompatible cursor contracts selected by an undocumented query param and the caller's identity: DateTimePaginator pages purely by offset (cursor.value used only for prev-edge trimming) while OptimizedCursorPaginator filters by cursor.value and also applies the offset, so a Link-header cursor emitted under one path and replayed under the other (client drops optimized_pagination=true when following the link, link shared with a non-superuser, or the is_superuser/global-access gate differs between callers) is reinterpreted under different semantics, producing skipped or duplicated rows — same route, same token, different results per caller, with no versioning and no documentation of the new param, breaking any client that caches or shares pagination links.

adjudication.rationale: The endpoint now conditionally selects two different paginator implementations based on `optimized_pagination=true` and caller privileges (`is_superuser` / `has_global_access`). This means the same route can emit cursors under one contract and later parse them under the other if the query param is omitted/changed or a different identity follows the link. The diff shows `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result()` uses `cursor.value` to `build_queryset(cursor_value, cursor.is_prev)` (i.e., value-based filtering) and then applies `cursor.offset`, while the existing paginator path shown at `paginator.py:get_result` slices primarily by `offset` and only uses `cursor.value` for prev-edge trimming. That mismatch can lead to skipped/duplicated rows when a cursor generated under one mode is replayed under the other, with no versioning/compat guard in the endpoint.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [P3] The cursors.py change is comment-only and misstates the input contract — comments at src/sentry/utils/cursors.py:26-27 claim negative offsets are now 'allowed ... for advanced pagination', but self.offset = int(offset) is byte-identical to before with no validation added and no behavior changed, documenting an externally reachable input contract that nothing implements while omitting the one coherent change (rejecting negative offsets in decode_cursor) that the negative-offset issues would actually have needed.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/utils/cursors.py` the only change is adding comments above `self.offset = int(offset)`, with no validation or behavioral change in `Cursor` itself (the assignment is unchanged). So the finding that this is a comment-only change that risks documenting an input/behavioral contract without implementing it is grounded in the diff. However, the finding’s claim about an omitted change in `decode_cursor` cannot be verified from the provided diff (no `decode_cursor` change is shown), and the wider diff *does* add/adjust negative-offset handling in paginator code, so the comment is not entirely untethered—just potentially misleading as to what changed where.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [P3] Paginator-specific constructor kwarg enable_advanced_features=True is pushed through the shared Endpoint.paginate() boundary at organization_auditlogs.py:82 — if paginate() does not forward arbitrary kwargs to the paginator constructor, this either raises TypeError (another 500 on the optimized path) or silently drops the flag, making the negative-offset branch at paginator.py ~877 permanently unreachable; needs verification against Endpoint.paginate's signature.

adjudication.rationale: In organization_auditlogs.py the optimized path calls self.paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, enable_advanced_features=True). The diff does not show Endpoint.paginate()’s signature or whether it forwards arbitrary kwargs to the paginator constructor, so it’s not verifiable from this diff whether this will raise a TypeError or silently ignore the flag. The concern is specific and diff-grounded but requires checking code outside the shown changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: In src/sentry/api/endpoints/organization_auditlogs.py:71, `organization_context` is never defined (the endpoint receives `organization`), so `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises NameError for every non-superuser (org owners, API-key clients) on every GET of the audit-logs endpoint — the line executes unconditionally (not gated by `use_optimized`) and only superusers avoid evaluating the second operand via `or` short-circuiting, causing a guaranteed 500 on this compliance-critical endpoint regardless of the optimized_pagination flag.

adjudication.rationale: The new code in `organization_auditlogs.py` introduces `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but in the shown diff hunk there is no prior definition of `organization_context`. This line is evaluated unconditionally (before the `if use_optimized and enable_advanced`), so if `organization_context` is indeed undefined in the surrounding function/module, it would raise `NameError` for any non-superuser request (since `or` would then evaluate the second operand).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Even setting the NameError aside, `.member.has_global_access` in that line matches no real permission attribute, and the endpoint's `OrganizationAuditPermission` already gates access, so the permission check is broken and redundant even in its intended form.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but `organization_context` is not defined anywhere in the shown endpoint, making this line a runtime `NameError` and breaking the new optimized pagination gating. The additional claim that `.member.has_global_access` is not a real attribute can’t be verified from the diff alone, but the check is definitely broken as introduced here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Django `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `AssertionError` ('Negative indexing is not supported') on negative slice bounds, so the paginator's negative-offset slicing (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` in the advanced branch at paginator.py ~888-891 and the unclamped `is_prev` paths at ~898 and ~182) always results in an unhandled 500 — the comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false, and since legitimate cursors never carry negative offsets (only forged, unsigned base64 cursors, which `Cursor.__init__` happily accepts negative ints for), the advertised negative-offset pagination feature is only reachable as a crash and can never return a successful response.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces (and in one path preserves) negative slicing into Django QuerySets. In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the “advanced” branch explicitly sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0` and then does `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Separately, `DateTimePaginator.get_result` was changed to clamp offsets only when `not cursor.is_prev`, leaving `start_offset = offset` (potentially negative) for `cursor.is_prev` and then slicing `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative bounds and raises an `AssertionError`, so these code paths can produce an unhandled 500; the comments claiming negative slicing is handled safely are therefore incorrect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` calls `self.build_queryset(cursor_value, cursor.is_prev)` (~858) as the first paginator call in `get_result`, but `build_queryset` was never copied or defined — it is a `DateTimePaginator` method not provided by `BasePaginator` — so every optimized request raises AttributeError immediately.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `OptimizedCursorPaginator` inherits `BasePaginator` and calls `self.build_queryset(...)`, but the diff does not show the definition of `BasePaginator` (or whether it provides `build_queryset`). Since we can’t verify from the diff alone that `build_queryset` is exclusive to `DateTimePaginator` or absent from `BasePaginator`, the claimed guaranteed `AttributeError` is not verifiable here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The `get_item_key` copied into `OptimizedCursorPaginator` dropped the datetime-to-number normalization its `DateTimePaginator` source has: with `order_by='-datetime'`, `math.floor(<datetime>)` / `math.ceil(<datetime>)` raises TypeError the first time it is invoked (prev-dedup at ~891 or inside `build_cursor`) on any non-empty page, and using key='id' instead would dedup/build cursors on `pk` while ordering by `datetime` — wrong keyset pagination, so no configuration of the copied code is correct.

adjudication.rationale: In `organization_auditlogs.py`, the optimized path calls `self.paginate(... paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, order_by="-datetime", ...)` without specifying a different key. `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` then does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` followed by `math.floor(value)` / `math.ceil(value)` and casts to `int`. With `order_by="-datetime"`, `self.key` will (by typical paginator behavior) correspond to the `datetime` attribute, and `math.floor/ceil` on a `datetime` value will raise `TypeError` on any non-empty page when building/deduping cursors. The diff provides no datetime-to-number normalization in `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, so this is a concrete runtime break introduced by the new paginator.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `enable_advanced_features=True` is passed to `Endpoint.paginate()` (organization_auditlogs.py:77-85), which has a fixed parameter list (`request, queryset, paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, count_hits, known_hits, max_hits`) and does not forward unknown kwargs to `paginator_cls`, raising TypeError before the paginator is even instantiated — an independent, earlier crash on the optimized path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True)` being passed on the optimized path in `organization_auditlogs.py`, but it does not include the definition/signature of `Endpoint.paginate()` or whether it accepts/forwards `**kwargs` to the paginator. The finding’s claim that `paginate()` has a fixed parameter list and will raise `TypeError` before instantiating the paginator is therefore not verifiable from the provided diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Double pagination in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` (paginator.py ~885-898): `build_queryset` applies a keyset filter truncating the queryset to rows past the cursor value, then the already-filtered queryset is offset-sliced (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`) while `build_cursor` advances the cursor's offset by `limit` every page — on page 2 the code slices `[limit : 2*limit]` of the rows older than the boundary, silently skipping the entire next page of audit entries.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` does both `build_queryset(cursor_value, ...)` and then slices with `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset` is derived from `cursor.offset`. However, the finding’s core claim—that `build_queryset` keyset-truncates the queryset *and* `build_cursor` “advances the cursor's offset by limit every page”, causing page-2 skipping—cannot be verified from this diff: neither `BasePaginator.build_queryset` nor `build_cursor` (and how they set `cursor.offset`) are shown. Without seeing that `cursor.offset` actually grows by `limit` (rather than typically remaining 0 except for tie-handling), the “silently skipping the entire next page” behavior is not provable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The prev-boundary dedup check `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` (paginator.py ~894) compares against a window that no longer matches the actual slice whenever clamping/negative offsets are in play, producing duplicate boundary rows.

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `cursor.is_prev and cursor.value` the code may slice with a negative `start_offset` (advanced branch uses `start_offset = cursor.offset` and `queryset[start_offset:stop]`). However the prev-boundary trimming condition still checks `len(results) == offset + limit + extra`. With negative offsets, `offset + limit + extra` no longer represents the slice window size (which is effectively `limit + extra` from the chosen `start_offset`), so the condition can fail to trigger and the extra boundary row won’t be dropped, causing duplicate/extra rows at page boundaries.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` change in shared `OffsetPaginator.get_result` (paginator.py ~181-185) silently masks invalid cursors: it is a no-op for all legitimate cursors (so the optimization does nothing for real traffic), but forged negative-offset cursors that previously triggered a loud `AssertionError`/500 are now silently clamped to 0 and return 200 OK with page-1 data while `build_cursor` keeps advancing the cursor chain from the unclamped negative offset, yielding repeated/duplicated pages and a corrupted cursor sequence; because this edits the shared `OffsetPaginator`, the blast radius is every offset-paginated endpoint in the API (members, projects, etc.), not just audit logs, and no boundary validation was added anywhere.

adjudication.rationale: In `paginator.py` the shared offset-based paginator logic was changed from slicing with `queryset[offset:stop]` to using `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` and then slicing `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. This demonstrably changes behavior for forged/invalid cursors with negative `offset` (when `cursor.is_prev` is false): instead of propagating a negative slice index (which Django typically rejects), it silently clamps to 0 and returns the first page. The cursor object still retains the original `cursor.offset` value (nothing in the diff normalizes/validates it), so downstream cursor construction can become inconsistent with the returned rows. Because this edit is in the shared paginator implementation, it affects all endpoints using this paginator, not just the audit log endpoint.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The clamping is inconsistent between the two branches of the same change: the forward path clamps negative offsets to 0 while the `is_prev` branch deliberately leaves them unclamped, so the identical forged input silently returns a 200 in one branch and still crashes with `AssertionError` in the other.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` the new slicing logic clamps `offset` only when `not cursor.is_prev` (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). If a forged/invalid cursor provides a negative `cursor.offset` with `cursor.is_prev=True`, `start_offset` remains negative and the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices and can raise `AssertionError` (negative indexing not supported). The forward-path clamps to 0 and would avoid that crash, so behavior differs by branch as the finding states.

adjudication_records.issue_text: On the same endpoint and URL, paginator selection (`DateTimePaginator` vs `OptimizedCursorPaginator`) depends on a client-controlled query param and the user's class, producing different cursor value encodings (raw passthrough vs normalized datetime keys) and offset semantics; a cursor minted by one path and replayed against the other (param toggled mid-pagination, or a shared/bookmarked URL) is silently misinterpreted — wrong pages, no error — and responses are non-reproducible across users for the same query.

adjudication.rationale: The endpoint now chooses `paginator_cls` based on a client-controlled `optimized_pagination=true` flag and `enable_advanced` (superuser/global access) (organization_auditlogs.py). That means the same URL/query can return cursors generated by different paginator implementations depending on user/param, but `self.paginate(...)` will still accept a `cursor` from the request without any guard that it was minted by the same paginator. Since different paginator classes can interpret `Cursor.value/offset` differently (new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor` is a raw passthrough and it also adds special negative-offset behavior), replaying/bookmarking a cursor across the other path can be silently misinterpreted, producing incorrect page boundaries without an explicit error.
